prompt.context: You are the CEO of a large multinational fast food chain called Crunch Yo' Burger. In recent years, you have noticed that your profitability in the US has been lagging behind competitors. Your Board of Directors would like to know why profitability is below that of competitors and how you plan to get profitability back in line. Your company sells fast food that is cooked onsite (similar price point to McDonald's/Subway). Crunch Yo' Burger operates all its own stores (no franchises). There are four major players in the market, differentiated only by the type of food they offer (prices are the same): Crunch Yo' Burger (hamburgers), TacoCo (tacos/Mexican food), NoodleCo (noodles), and PizzaCo (pizzas). We are concerned only with US operations. Customers can be either takeout or eat-in.
prompt.question: Why is Crunch Yo' Burger's profitability in the US lagging behind competitors, and how do you plan to get it back in line?

clarifying_info.q: Can you share detailed figures on profit or revenue?
clarifying_info.a: I will show you an exhibit after I have seen your structure.
This is a price-sensitive market; prices have been largely flat across all players.

clarifying_info.q: Does Crunch Yo' Burger franchise any stores?
clarifying_info.a: No, Crunch Yo' Burger operates all its own stores.

clarifying_info.q: Are we looking at US only?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, we are concerned only with the US operations of Crunch Yo' Burger and its competitors.

exhibits.title: Revenue and Profits (US only) — 2017 & 2018
exhibits.shows: A chart presenting 2017 and 2018 revenues for all four competitors (Crunch Yo' Burger, TacoCo, NoodleCo, PizzaCo), 2018 net profits in absolute terms for each player, and 2018 variable costs broken out as food variable costs and non-food variable costs expressed as a percentage of sales for each player.
exhibits.data: Crunch Yo' Burger has the highest revenue (~$20B in 2018); all players grew ~10% from 2017 to 2018; Crunch Yo' Burger 2018 net profit ~$200M (~1% margin); competitors net profit margins ~1.5-2%; non-food variable costs: Crunch Yo' Burger 11% of sales vs competitors ~10% of sales; food variable costs are similar across players.

framework: Revenue: Price x Quantity x Product mix
Revenue drivers: price changes, volume/market share, product mix, bundling, upselling
External market: market growth, competitor actions, new entrants, health trends, regulation
Variable costs: food costs (raw ingredients) and non-food variable costs (packaging, condiments, consumables)
Fixed costs: rental, labour, utilities — long-term contracts, branch openings/closures

questions.prompt: After presenting your structure, you are handed Exhibit 1. What does it tell you, and where should you focus?
questions.guidance: Candidate should: (1) note Crunch Yo' Burger is market leader by revenue; (2) observe ~10% revenue growth is consistent across all players — not a revenue issue; (3) convert net profit to margins to compare apples-to-apples (~1% for Crunch Yo' Burger vs 1.5-2% for peers, a ~0.5% gap worth ~$100M); (4) identify that the margin gap is driven by non-food variable costs (11% of sales vs ~10% for peers); (5) recommend focusing the investigation on non-food variable costs.

math.setup: Compare net profit margins: Net profit / Revenue. Crunch Yo' Burger ~$200M / ~$20B = 1%. Competitor range ~1.5-2%. Gap ~0.5% of ~$20B revenue.
steps: 0.5% x $20B = $100M gap attributable to non-food variable costs
Non-food variable cost difference: 11% - 10% = 1% of sales; but net impact on profit is ~0.5% after accounting for scale
math.answer: Crunch Yo' Burger has ~$100M lower profit than if it matched peer non-food variable cost ratio.

questions.prompt: We have identified that non-food variable costs are the issue. What are some creative ways Crunch Yo' Burger could decrease these costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm non-food variable cost categories and reduction levers. Key categories: condiments (ketchup packets/dispensers), packaging (burger wrappers, soda cups), other consumables (napkins, toilet paper, plastic cutlery, hand sanitizer). Strong answers will propose specific operational interventions. Interviewer should steer towards napkins as a high-potential solution to set up the calculation question.

questions.prompt: Crunch Yo' Burger is considering purchasing a napkin dispensing machine (dispenses napkins one by one). One machine is needed per store and must be replaced every 2 years at $1,000 per machine. Currently customers take ~5 napkins each from a large stack; the machine would reduce this to 2 napkins per customer. This solution applies only to eat-in customers. How much money can Crunch Yo' Burger save per year by implementing this machine? Structure your inputs first, then calculate.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify all inputs before calculating: (1) number of stores, (2) number of eat-in customers per store per day, (3) reduction in napkins per customer, (4) cost per napkin, (5) days per year, (6) cost of machines. Then compute gross saving and subtract machine cost. Short version: give 22,500 stores and 960 sit-in customers/store/day. Long version: candidate estimates these (see optional estimations).

math.setup: Net saving = (Napkins saved per customer x Customers per store per day x Cost per napkin x Days per year x Number of stores) - Annual machine cost. Napkins saved = 5 - 2 = 3. Cost per napkin = $28 / 6000 = ~$0.005 (half a cent). Annual machine cost = $1000 / 2 years = $500 per store; total = $500 x 22,500 = ~$11M.
steps: Gross saving per store per year = 3 napkins x 960 customers x $0.005 x 365 days = 3 x 960 x 0.005 x 365
= 3 x 960 = 2,880 napkins saved per store per day
2,880 x $0.005 = $14.40 saved per store per day
$14.40 x 365 = ~$5,256 saved per store per year

brainstorming.prompt: We have calculated that implementing the napkin machine saves ~$106M per year, bringing our margin from 1% to ~1.5%. What are some other ways we could save on non-food variable costs?

categories.name: Condiments
ideas: Limit ketchup to 1 packet per order and charge for extras
Replace individual ketchup packets with a self-serve ketchup dispenser
Apply similar dispensing logic to straws and sugar sachets

categories.name: Packaging
ideas: Use cheaper or lighter packaging materials (with environmental/brand risk trade-off)
Switch to recyclable or compostable packaging to reduce waste fees
Standardize cup sizes to reduce SKU complexity and bulk-buy at lower cost

categories.name: Consumables
ideas: Hand out napkins at the counter (controlled distribution) rather than leaving stacks out
Install napkin dispensing machines (the focus solution)
Reduce toilet paper by installing dispensers that dispense limited sheets
Reduce plastic cutlery waste by only including cutlery when requested

categories.name: Purchasing / Supply chain
ideas: Centralize purchasing across all stores to capture bulk discounts
Source cheaper napkins or other consumables without compromising hygiene

categories.name: Operational efficiency
ideas: Extend the useful life of reusable utensils (trays, baskets)
Reduce over-ordering of consumables that expire or spoil

recommendation: Our lower profitability is caused by high non-food variable costs — specifically excessive napkin usage by eat-in customers.
We recommend implementing napkin dispensing machines across all 22,500 US stores, reducing napkins taken per customer from 5 to 2 (a 60% reduction).
This initiative saves ~$106M per year net of machine costs, increasing our net profit margin from 1% to ~1.5% — bringing us within the range of our competitors.
risks: Customer experience risk: the machine may frustrate customers accustomed to freely available napkins.
Operational risk: machine jams or maintenance delays could slow service.
Brand/PR risk: perceived cost-cutting could harm brand perception if not communicated well.
next_steps: Pilot the napkin dispensing machine in ~100 stores nationwide and collect customer feedback before full rollout.
Pursue similar dispensing or rationing initiatives for ketchup and straws to further close the profitability gap.
Investigate raw material bulk discounts and renegotiate supplier contracts on key consumables.
